item.title: Dumping Deuce Not Advised
item.author: John Gove
item.content:encoded: Seasoned Knicks fans have doctorate degrees in roster construction, with a primary focus on asset management. For over a decade, we spent countless hours discussing expiring contracts, tracking picks, and praying the day would come when all the “futures thinking” translated into a legitimate championship window.Well, we made it. Like the driver-side door on my red Nissan Rogue, the window is now open. But now that repeating as champions is the goal, New York’s roster-building approach is shifting again. That shift directly brings our focus to Miles “Deuce” McBride and his future with the Knicks.Entering the final year of his contract, it is no secret that talks between Deuce and the Knicks have stalled. All signs point to him wanting to stay in New York. The fan base would love him to remain as a key piece of the rotation. However, ownership and the front office are fretting about wearing two aprons while making their prize-winning pizza, especially with Jim Dolan looking over their shoulders. Because of that fearful culinary attire (too many second-apron jokes?), a growing segment of the fanbase is convinced the Knicks must flip him before the trade deadline. Whether it’s to recoup a draft pick or fill a worrisome hole at center, Deuce cannot simply walk away for nothing. OK, sure he can. And maybe he does. Regardless, trading him away because of that worry would be a majorly short-sighted mistake.New York finds itself in a bit of a financial gridlock. After sacrificing about $113M to help the team, Brunson will be extension eligible next summer (). Anunoby and Bridges are secure for now (on ascending contracts), Hart would like to extend now, and throw in a monster contract for Towns, and there’s not much wiggle room.In the old NBA, James Dolan could scribble out a luxury-tax check to keep a fan favorite around. Then the 2023 CBA introduced a first apron (roughly $8–9M above the tax line) and a second apron (roughly $17–21M+ above the tax line, depending on the year; e.g., ~$221.7M for 2026-27). Crossing that damned second apron doesn’t just trigger a tax penalty; it hijacks a team’s roster-building. If you cross the line, you lose trade flexibility, the ability to aggregate salaries, and future first-round picks get frozen like Jack Dawson at the end of .Unfortunately, Deuce is a potential casualty of math. He’ll undoubtedly earn a significant pay raise in his next contract. However, the Knicks can’t give him one without dismantling a starting five that just brought New York a championship… and appeared on Saturday Night Live. He isn’t a financial priority because the money could be spent more intelligently elsewhere. That’s just the reality of the business.So, if the Knicks probably cannot pay the guy, why not trade him now? Well, that answer has two parts. First, what he does on the court can’t be easily replaced. Second, he gets paid very little (relatively speaking) to do it.Deuce is making a “meager” $3.96 million this season. That kind of contract is a cheat code for a contending team. In the trade market, however, it is a major limitation. An outgoing $4 million salary doesn’t bring back a game-changing asset. Consider how Deuce’s skill set impacts New York’s production on both ends of the court. Averaging 12 points per game last year and shooting roughly 40% from three, he spaces the floor well with Brunson and punishes defenses that try to double the captain. Defensively, he is relentless at the point of attack. He picks up opposing guards full court, navigates ball screens, and takes on the most tiresome defensive assignment to give the primary producers a break. You cannot find that level of two-way reliability for under $4 million.But John… We desperately need a center!I mean, you’re not entirely wrong. Big Mitch is gone and glancing at the center depth chart is enough to raise anyone’s blood pressure. Looking at Deuce as the best trade chip is tempting and convincing yourself we can flip him for a big man is quite easy to do. But trading an elite rotational guard for a stopgap center that potentially might not play a whole lot is terrible roster management. Do the math for a minute. If we trade Deuce’s contract, we have to bring back a $4 million center. That gets the Knicks a deepl flawed, third-string big man destined to get hunted in the pick-and-roll and become nonexistent come playoff time. Anyone willing to trade a guy who plays closing minutes in crucial games for a big who will consistently rock the warmup gear should not be employed by an NBA front office. New York can survive the early schedule by signing a low-cost option and patch the center rotation by committee, and even have OG play a little five (as Mike Brown even mentioned.) It gives them time to evaluate the landscape and see what shakes out throughout the league. Panicking in October and trading our best bench piece does nothing but hurts the organization’s title odds. There is also precedent to consider. The Knicks brass were probably well-aware that they would not be able to afford to re-sign Mitchell Robinson this summer—and his departure is the reason why we’re in this pickle at center. Leon Rose must have heard some interest in Mitch before the in-season trade deadline, but he held on to the asset. Unless there’s a – we suspect he’ll do the same with Deuce.Forward-thinking got the Knicks where they are today. Focussing on the present is how they hang another championship banner up in Madison Square Garden for the second straight year. Letting a talented, 26-year-old guard hit unrestricted free agency without getting anything in return goes against everything we have been conditioned to believe. It might sting a little but the ultimate goal of asset management isn’t to pretty up the perfect spreadsheet. It is to win a championship. Miles McBride helps this roster win games this season.If we have to accept the 2026-27 campaign is essentially a one-year, rental of Deuce, so be it. Keep him on the roster! Let him lock down the opposition and hit clutch threes for us as we look for two in a row. If another franchise throws $20 million at him next summer, we simply song that catchy Fall Out Boy song and tell the man, “Thanks for the memories.” The window for winning is right now. You don’t close it early just to save a few bucks and appease the armchair analysts.

item.title: 'We'll show people we can train in short sleeves all year round' – Why the first-ever Vuelta a las Islas Canarias stage race is finally happening next January
item.author: Alasdair Fotheringham
item.content:encoded: The arrival of a new race of any description always sparks interest amongst fans, but when it is set to open the UCI pro racing calendar for the year, like the new Vuelta a las Islas Canarias will do next January, there's arguably even more intrigue.Set to be run for four days from January 14-17, the Canary Islands stage race will be the first ever to be held on the Spanish archipelago, situated roughly 1,000 kilometres south of the mainland and frequently used by both professionals and amateurs alike for warm weather and altitude training camps.According to promoter and organiser Noelia Pérez, the idea of the stage race was partly born out of wanting to showcase the popularity of the sport in the islands - and the reasons for that popularity. But it was also designed to provide a focal point for riders from the Canaries who don't get the opportunity to witness top-level pro racing so often, given the distances involved between the islands and the Spanish peninsula."It's an idea that was born a long time ago, because it's a bit of a shout-out for the cycling world about the Canary Islands," Pérez tells "I'm also president of a club which operates at national level which has juniors and juveniles all from the Canaries, called Gran Canaria Bike Team and then at U23 level in conjunction with a Basque squad. Then there are other flourishing clubs throughout the Canaries, like Tenerife Bike Point and Tenerife ViClass and so on."Basically, there are a lot of kids here who dream about being professional. But being in the Canaries, as you can imagine, it's really hard to travel across to the mainland and get all the infrastructure there, like the team vehicles, material and so on. "So for the last four years we've had a base on the mainland and another one here and they race around 25 events a year outside the Canaries."But at the same time, the club begin putting on races in the Canaries too, including a two-day U18 race in one of the two main islands, Tenerife, and then another, the U23 Vuelta al Norte in the other, Gran Canaria. The next step was the Canary Islands' first-ever pro race, with an eye not just on the racers back home, but also on the international cycling market."They're promoting cyclo-tourism here a lot, and a lot of the pro teams come here to train as well to prepare at altitude," Pérez points out. The consistently warm climate plays a key role in encouraging bike riders to travel to the Canaries, as well as the increasing interest from the public authorities in promoting sustainable tourism."Combine the two - that interest in the younger riders in the sport and the public authorities' interest in promoting it, and the race was able to come to life."The decision to hold the race so early in the year was deliberately taken as a way of showcasing that it's possible to ride in pleasant conditions in the Canary Islands no matter the season, Pérez says."Here we train in short sleeves and shorts 365 days of the year," she said, "and we wanted to show that. You have to see that to believe that.""Plus there's a lot of racing in Australia and the Middle East at that time of year, but this is for those who've stayed in Europe who say 'Ooh, let's go and find some warm weather in the Canary Islands'. Because if they're on the rollers training indoors on the mainland because of the cold, we've got what we call 'the eternal spring' here."Being the first race of the year also shows people what they can do in the Canary Islands as well."Other advantages of holding the race so early in the season are that teams would be able to combine their winter training camps on the islands with the race itself. Another added incentive is that, in keeping with the first road events of the year, the race itself would not be overly demanding. No Mount Teide... for nowThere are certainly no plans, at least initially, to go up the Mount Teide volcano - Spain's highest mountain, peaking out at 3,715 metres above sea level - Pérez agrees with a smile before adding good-humouredly: "They'd kill us; nobody would come.""It's not out of the question, if we ended up being WorldTour or changing dates. But that's a long way away for now." Rather the initial format is comparatively low-key, she says: although starts and finish towns are yet to be released for 2027, what's already decided is there will be four mass start stages on relatively easy terrain, and no time trials. As for the initial four-day structure, the reason is geographic, given there are two main regions in the Canaries, the northerly one including Gran Canaria, Lanzarote, Isla Graciosa and Fuerteventura and the southerly one including Tenerife, La Palma, La Gomera and Hierro. Support will be provided by the OCETA organisation, which currently runs Itzulia Basque Country and San Sebastián.With the race having both public and private funding, the current plan is to have two stages in each of the biggest islands, although in the mid-term, the race would be run over six of the biggest islands, using ferries or planes to transport the riders and infrastructure from one to another.Given the multiple points of interest for holding a bike race - and in in the first 24 hours after the race was published on the UCI's website, teams are already contacting Pérez to find out more details, she says - the biggest question about the Vuelta a las Islas Canarias is perhaps not so much why it is happening for the first time now. Rather it's why it hasn't happened before. That's even more surprising, given virtually every region in Spain has or has had its local stage race, right down to the smallest regions like Murcia and - back in the day - La Rioja. "The fact that we were going to have the Vuelta here has shown people just how much interest there is in the sport here. But our own regional tour is totally compatible with having the Vuelta a España here some day, and the authorities are still keen to have it happen here on the islands. They still want to do it.""The good news is that whatever happens about the Vuelta, we've got our own regional tour happening now. And if it's happening now, that's because the different political institutions and the parties have all come together with the same idea about it. "Without that official support it wouldn't be able to happen. And that's really good news, because that kind of cross-party agreement doesn't happen that often about anything."Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of both the UCI Road and Gravel World Championships, alongside the final monument of the season, Il Lombardia. item.title: Tadej Pogačar and Urška Žigart arrive home in Slovenia ahead of European Championships, despite injuries ruling them out of the racing
item.author: James Moultrie
item.content:encoded: Having both returned to training in recent weeks, Pogačar and Žigart trained near the capital city alongside Danish rider Mikkel Honoré, who is fresh off the back of finishing 19th in the Road World Championships in Montreal, Canada.After his season-ending crash at the Vuelta a España on August 29, speculation returned this week about whether the defending men's road race champion Pogačar would, after all, be able to make it back in time from his neck and collarbone fractures and concussion to race on home roads.Pogačar made a rare appearance in the European Champion's white jersey on Honoré's Instagram story, with its blue bands and gold stars on show. He had worn the World Champion's jersey in races and training until last Sunday, when trade teammate Brandon McNulty succeeded him in Montreal. The 196.3km race will pass near Pogačar's hometown of Komenda, before reaching the laps of the finishing circuit into Šenčur. With Pogačar not defending his title, Remco Evenepoel (Belgium) will start as the heavy favourite, with Primož Roglič and Jakob Omrzel representing Slovenia's best chances in the absence of their and the sport's top rider. For Žigart, it was a re-fractured jaw that has seen her miss out on the chance to represent her country on home roads. She sustained the injury during a crash at the Faun Tour Femmes, having already broken her jaw earlier this season at the Tour de Suisse.Without her, Slovenia will be fielding a three-rider team for Saturday's road race: current road and TT National Champion Nika Bobnar, Špela Kern, and Tjaša Sušnik. Having been unable to start in Ljubljana, it's unlikely we see either rider fully back in action until the start of the 2027 season. The last race which could entice Pogačar is, of course, Il Lombardia, where he has won the past five titles in a row, but with UAE's messaging ever since he crashed that recovery and health are the priority for their star rider, it would be a long shot to see him starting in Bergamo on October 10.Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of both the UCI Road and Gravel World Championships, alongside the final monument of the season, Il Lombardia. item.title: Magicshine Monteer 12000 review: A bike light that boasts more beam power than any other model
item.author: Paul Burwell
item.content:encoded: £459.99 / $499.99 / €495.99 Lamp 300g, battery 897gHigh, medium, low, eco12,000, 6,000, 3,000, 1,000 10,000 mAh Li-ion 2.1, 7, 11.5, 37hrsMagicshine has built a reputation for offering great-value lights for bikes, but it's been ramping up the power and tech in its more recent models.The Monteer 12000 is the most powerful light the brand has ever made and is also the brightest bike light on the market. But how does it fare out in the real world, and does anyone really need a 12000-lumen bike light with twice the output as the brightest of its rivals? We tested the Monteer 12000 out on the trails to find out.Design and specificationsMagicshine stacks five LEDs in the Monteer 12000’s aluminium lamp unit, combining a large central spot with four smaller angled units. The lamp has a simple on/off switch and you can toggle between the flood and spot beams or power up both. To save you from reaching over to adjust, the light comes with a bar-mounted remote, which is already bound into the light. There’s a little bit of sequencing to access the different options, requiring you to double-press the remote to go from the flashing modes to the dedicated mountain bike modes, but once sorted, you can then toggle up and down quickly. To allow some further customisation, Magicshine also has a dedicated light app for both iOS and Android. You do have to reconnect the light each time via Bluetooth and the app is a little clunky to use, but you can do a full custom tune.The lamp unit is mounted in a machined aluminium twin clamp, which straddles the front of the stem. It fits 35mm bars out of the box, but shims are provided for smaller bar diameters. The cells that make up the 14.4V 10,000mAh battery are all housed inside a durable plastic case. This has a slight profile, so it sits relatively neatly against a frame tube and is secured via two Velcro-backed straps. If you press the button on the side of the battery, it illuminates a small fuel gauge. This has four bars, which roughly equates to 22 percent for each bar, with the last 10 percent shown as a flashing red bar. This isn’t as accurate as a percentage figure, but it’s a bit easier to see when in the saddle.On the end of the battery pack is an input for the power cable and another for the USB-C charging cable. The system comes with a 600mm cable and a 900mm extension in the box, alongside a plastic helmet mount and two mounting straps. So if you have the neck strength, you can run this beast on your helmet.With its twin clamp, the Monteer 12000 is way more solid compared to the Monteer 6000, which uses a single-sided mount. This eliminates a lot of vibration and it’s also a hinged design, so you can attach it without moving the controls or grip. The fixing bolts are also on the top for ease of access. By loosening the small lever on one side, you can pivot the lamp in the clamp on the trail – but unfortunately, we snapped this on our sample. There is a small hex bolt on the opposite side that does a similar job, but how long this will last is unknown. The beam pattern produced by the Monteer 12000 isn’t quite as smooth as some, and there is a definite hard edge between the flooded areas and the spot beam. It’s not quite as white or as crisp as Exposure's lights, but picking out the detail is never an issue. The amount of light on full beam is insane, and you can see as far and as wide as you want.In tight trees and dense undergrowth, there’s quite a bit of bounce back, so I often rode in the medium 6,000 lumen setting in the trees and on climbs. That way you can also extend the 2.2hr run time on full beam to over seven hours. The battery is big enough to do the whole of the night portion of a 24hr race on a single charge, but one of the downsides is it will take most of the rest of the day to recharge. With so much power going into the lamp, it also gets pretty hot. To keep it as cool as possible there's an air intake at the front of the light and an exhaust port at the rear, as well as a couple of cooling fins. But if you’re worried, you can also monitor the temperature via the app. The clamp design allows you to mount the lamp below the level of the stem keeping the weight low, but that tool-free adjustment needs to be a bolt, one that you can replace easily if damaged. I’d also like to see wider Velcro straps for the battery and a more integrated system for the remote mounting. With this amount of output for this amount of money, the Monteer 12000 is very impressive. If you’re hitting 30 to 40mph down a gravel road descent at night, its got your back on full powerHowever, from a purely practical point of view, toggling down to 6,000 or even 3,000 lumens means you can get seriously good run times, and that's how I use it most of the time. Plus, the lower settings mean you don’t have to battle glare bouncing back from objects ahead of you, and they are still bright enough for rapid off-road night rides.

item.title: The reasons behind Alonso renewing F1 contract with Aston Martin
'We'll continue to race as we always do' – Brandon McNulty says new world champion status won't change his racing approach
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: The American is heading to Italy to take on a host of late-season Classics to end his 2026 campaign, with Saturday's Giro dell'Emilia marking his first race in the world champion's jersey.He'll head up a strong UAE squad with Jhonatan Narváez, Tim Wellens, Adam Yates, Filippo Baroncini, Felix Großschartner, and Igor Arrieta at the race, which marks his first time at the Italian Classics since 2021."I still have a lot of racing left this season, and I'm excited for it. We have a strong group for these races, and we'll be aggressive as always," McNulty said."While I'm honoured to wear the rainbow jersey, it doesn't change my approach. We'll continue to race as we always do."Whether that's attacking or helping my teammates – I know my role pretty well, and we have a great understanding of what works, so we'll keep it that way."McNulty should wear the number one dossard as team leader this weekend, though realistically any one of him, Narváez, Wellens, and Yates could contend for the hilly race in Bologna, which features five ascents of the famous San Luca hill overlooking the city.He and his teammates will hope to keep the title within his team, as Tadej Pogačar and Isaac del Toro have won the race in the past two seasons. Other top contenders at the race include Tom Pidcock (Pinarello-Q36.5), Mikel Landa (Soudal-QuickStep), and Ben Healy (EF Education-EasyPost).After the Giro dell'Emilia, McNulty will round out his season with three more Italian one-dayers: the Coppa Agostoni on Sunday before racing Tre Valli Varesine on Tuesday and Il Lombardia next Saturday."I'm really excited to make my debut in the rainbow jersey this Saturday," McNulty said."The win in Montreal has definitely been something massive for me, and I am still coming to terms with it a bit and letting it sink in."Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of both the UCI Road and Gravel World Championships, alongside the final Monument of the season, Il Lombardia. Subscribers get unlimited access to exclusive analysis from our expert columnists, in-depth features and industry-leading tech insight. Plus, the Cyclingnews app lets you follow the action wherever you go!

Cycling has the fans, it just needs to monetise them – Can a new style of events and engagement help to solve cycling's funding problem?
item.author: Emma Magnus
item.content:encoded: It is scorchingly hot at the Cheer Squad corner, five kilometres from the summit of Mont Ventoux. The Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift is due to pass through within the hour, and excitement is building. To the right, there is a screen where a cluster of people have gathered to watch the race; to the left, there is a sea of polka-dot-T-shirt-clad bodies dancing to Freed from Desire and waving flags which flutter in the blue sky. On the road itself, huge painted letters read: "WATCH THE FEMMES".There are almost 200 people on this one corner, most of whom have cycled the first 15 kilometres up the mountain – and many, like me, have completed the 112-kilometre L'Étape du Tour de France Femmes the day before. Both L'Étape, which attracted a record 10,500 participants – up 70% on 2025 – and the Cheer Squad, organised by ex-pro Iris Slappendel, have helped to bring thousands of extra fans to the roadside to watch the stage, turning a day-long event into a full weekend. The Tour de France, of course, is the biggest race in the sport – but not all races, particularly at lower levels, are experiencing the same turnout. The Tour de L'Avenir Femmes was put on hold this year, while the Tour de Romandie Féminin was postponed until 2027. This month, the women's Tour of Guangxi was cancelled and removed from the UCI calendar, its future uncertain. On the men's side, the Maryland Cycling Classic, Tour of Norway and first edition of a new stage race, Lyon-Turin, were all cancelled this year due to funding issues. Cycling, which depends on sponsorship, has a precarious financial model, and with operational costs rising, teams and race organisers are scrambling to keep up. To advocacy organisation The Cyclists' Alliance (TCA), events like these are part of the solution. "It is our view that the greatest untapped opportunity for both men's and women's cycling lies in generating revenue through festival-style events built around races," the organisation wrote in an open letter to the UCI in April. "The potential to increase revenue by enhancing and monetising the fan experience is substantial". 'Fan engagement' was one of the key areas of a UCI consultation earlier this year, and it is one of the five pillars the governing body recently laid out in its 'Future of Cycling' manifesto. 51% of respondents to the consultation touched on promotion, and ideas proposed in the manifesto included "new race formats for fan engagement: urban-circuit races, mixed-team time trials, combined road and gravel events, and formats linking professional races to mass-participation events."Events can boost spectator appeal, generate income, raise sponsorship value and bring people to the destination for longer, which has a positive knock-on effect for the local authorities that provide funding. Fans, the TCA argued, are central to the sustainability of the sport: without them, it cannot survive. The idea is not new. It re-emerged last year when there were discussions about whether parts of Alpe d'Huez should be ticketed at this year's Tour de France. Wout van Aert told : "I think that fragility would be much less of an issue if, alongside sponsorship income, there were also revenues coming from the sport itself." In the end, race organisers ASO rejected the idea, telling Belgian newspaper : "Cycling is free [for spectators] and bringing in a ticketing system is absolutely not on the current agenda.""It's bizarre that a sport where so many people do it doesn't have a bigger fanbase," explains Deena Blacking, TCA's interim managing director. "In cycling, we just don't have the event venue, merchandise and loyalty to the team that they do in football. That was the point that we made in the letter: these things can be overcome if there's the will and the effort. You can still do a road cycling race outside, but you can put it on circuits, and you can have it finish in a velodrome so that you can ticket bits of the course. Or you can create a VIP experience, or a spectator experience that is objectively interesting - as opposed to subjectively appealing to the die-hard cycling fan."So: what does it take to organise these kinds of fan events – and are they a way to make cycling more sustainable?From grassroots fan events to race organisers harnessing their powerWhen we speak, Slappendel has spent the last two days up Ventoux in preparation for the Cheer Squad, painting the road under cover of darkness. "There's too much traffic [in the day]," she explains. "And of course it's not really legal, but nobody cares." Slappendel, who retired from pro cycling in 2016 and now runs an apparel brand, started the Cheer Squad in 2024. Initially, the idea was to get people interested in women's racing, make it easier to watch, and to start a community around it. "When I was racing, there were not loads of people on the side of the road, but it's special when people cheer you on. I wanted to give that back to the peloton," she says. "I think the best way to support women's sport is to show up."The first year, around 50 people turned up on La Redoute. Last year, on the Col du Granier, there were around 80. And this year, on Ventoux, there were some 180. In future, she wants a Cheer Squad at every stage of the Tour de France Femmes, as well as at different races. "Every year we see more people coming," says Slappendel, who is being pulled away for a segment. "It's important for the riders, but also for the organisers, the broadcasters – it's good that everyone sees that there's an appetite for it. People show up; they travel to fucking Mont Ventoux because they love to watch the women's race."In-person fan events are growing throughout the sport. TNT Sports aired live from London for the first time during this year's Giro d'Italia, while events like LeBlanq's Joyride Festival, where fans can rub shoulders with cycling greats, have exploded in popularity. Teams like Visma-Lease a Bike, EF Education-Cannondale and Lidl-Trek sell hospitality and travel packages which offer access to the riders, or VIP race experiences. Riders are even hosting their own events: Rigoberto Uran started the Giro de Rigo in 2018; Canyon-SRAM rider Tiffany Cromwell has founded a series of gravel events, and Soudal Quick-Step's Gianmarco Garofoli runs 'Gianmarco Garofoli Day' in his hometown, featuring a ride, lunch and a prize draw. Clearly, there is community – and potentially revenue – to be gained from gathering people in-person.No race organiser knows this better than Flanders Classics, which took over the running of races like Omloop Het Nieuwsblad, Dwars door Vlaanderen and the Tour of Flanders in 2009. In 2023, Flanders Classics became a shareholder of Cycling Unlimited, which runs the Tour de Suisse, and in 2025, Amstel Gold also came under their umbrella. "The general idea was to bundle rights, governance and commercial opportunities to protect the spring Classics," says CEO Tomas Van Den Spiegel. "It's easy to organise the Tour of Flanders every year because it's super popular and everyone wants to be there, but there were a couple of other races that were trying to find their place in the international calendar, and maybe on the verge of losing importance. Bundling them with the Tour of Flanders and [Gent-]Welvelgem, for example, gave the other races an extra boost and helped them to be the races that they are today."The company rejigged some of the courses to maximise the spectator experience – "we tried to create experiences where cycling fans have something to look forward to all day, not just 30 seconds" – and now runs up to 70 cycling events a year. This includes amateur races, rides and sportives, hospitality packages and free fan villages at key points like the Oude Kwaremont, Paterberg and Koppenberg. Flanders Classics co-organises a dance festival, Démarrage, alongside the Tour of Flanders, with food trucks, big screens and DJs. This year, it introduced the FLCS Clubhouse in Ghent, with a five-day programme of talks, rides, runs and events to entice a newer, younger and "hipper" cycling audience. "It was more of an experiment," says Van Den Spiegel. "We will do it again next spring."Many of these events are free, with hospitality packages costing between €150 and around €500, says Van Den Spiegel. "The fact that cycling is so tangible, so close to the people – and that it's free – gives it its popularity. That's something you cannot touch," he says. "The major part of cycling will always remain free."Nevertheless, running these kinds of events is expensive. "It's not as simple as just throwing up a festival. It's something that we had to build, and it requires investment first," says Van Den Spiegel. Even with ticketing, it is hard to cover the costs of organisation. "We don't have stadiums or permanent set-ups, so you always have to start from scratch. You cannot underestimate the investment that you have to make to build festival-like fan zones."In 2025, some 2.45 million people attended the 10 Classics races under the organisation's charge, with 1.1 million people turning up for the Tour of Flanders. Races like Dwars door Vlaanderen and De Brabantse Pijl attracted 80,000 and 85,000 fans respectively. With these numbers, having designated fan zones can help with crowd control, dispersing spectators along the route. "The popularity of our races has multiplied. If you look at TV images of the early days and you compare them to today, there's no comparison," says Van Den Spiegel. "Some of these standalone races would be struggling today, [but] this type of platform allows them to be part of something bigger, and that's why they're still there."Not only do tourists stick around for longer, but the races bring visitors to Flanders year-round. According to Van Den Spiegel, Kluisbergen, the municipality where the Kwaremont and Paterberg are located, has 600 more tourist beds than in 2016. The local population is just 7,000. "Some of these municipalities are small, but they give us all of the logistical support needed and they really embrace the races. Some of the bigger cities support us financially as well," he says. "I think everyone's seeing the added value that embracing the spring Classics has given them."Flanders Classics' events calendar is an important part of its business model, creating a strong brand, providing opportunities for sponsors and partners – and generating income. Most revenue from events and hospitality goes towards covering the cost of running the races. "We're trying to build an A-brand, and eventually we will attract A-brands," says Van Den Spiegel. "The reality today is that we are quite stable. The fact that we have built these identities around these races and projects, and that people know what to expect, helps when you're selling your story."It is not just race organisers taking this approach. For the Unibet Rose Rockets, physical fan events are part of the team's DNA. In 2021, when co-founders Bas Tietema, Devin van der Wiel and Josse Wester ran the Tour de Tietema YouTube channel, they signed Wester up for his first amateur race in a 500-inhabitant village in the Netherlands. "At 10am on a Sunday morning, 2,000 people showed up to see Josse racing his first race," says Van der Wiel. "You can call it the first event of the whole project. We saw that there wasn't something like this in cycling, where fans show up during the race to support the team."When the Rockets was founded in 2023, therefore, they hosted their first team presentation with a circus tent, DJs, games and quizzes. "There were like 300 people there for a Conti team before we even had a race," says Van der Wiel.Nowadays, the team runs around four big fan events per year. They held coffee rides before Omloop het Nieuwsblad and the Tour of Flanders, ran ticketed bus trips to Paris-Roubaix and set up a Rockets Corner at Amstel Gold Race. This had a barbecue, stage with DJs, bands and singers, a quiz, partner and merch stalls, and a big screen. During the race's own amateur ride the day before, they set up a barber shop with Philips OneBlade, one of their sponsors, for riders to shave their legs. The Rockets Corner drew some 2,000 attendees, who cheered the team's breakaway rider on the race's first passage – evidence, says Van der Wiel, that "cycling can be more than just cheering for the winner"."I don't think the [race] organisers expected that amount of people," he says. "We were by far the smallest team at the race, but we had the biggest fan event. In big races, you see groups supporting a rider, but you don't see that much with a team. We want to build a community around the team, and events, of course, are a big part of that. Physical events are the things that you don't forget as a kid."Like with Flanders Classics, the Rockets' events are mostly free for fans to attend, which requires a "long-term investment". Although it provides an opportunity for partners to connect with their core audience, these events are less about directly monetizing the fanbase, and more about community building. "You invest in your fans; you invest in a connection with people that want to follow you, that trust you, that want to be part of the team and the journey. In the long-term, that can be really valuable for partners as well," he explains. "[We want to be] more than just a cycling team."Fan events, of course, are only one part of cycling's ecosystem – but, clearly, they hold power. "It's a jigsaw puzzle that needs to be addressed in tandem," says Blacking. "It has to be part of the overall modernisation of the fan experience, which includes the broadcast as well.""Everything starts with course design," adds Van Den Spiegel. Circuits, or loops where parts of the course are repeated – ideally at least three times – can help to keep spectators entertained all day, he says. "We focus on giving each race its own identity – different landmarks, different fan zones – to make sure that we don't cannibalize what we have today, and to keep those races as high on the cycling fans' calendar as possible."Can fan events help to solve cycling's funding problem, then? "I would say yes, but only if it's part of a bigger fan experience," says Van der Wiel. Improvements in broadcasting are still due, he argues, and cycling needs to be easier to follow and more accessible. "I think sport is something you do for the fans. You do it for people to enjoy; to inspire people; to make people care about you. Playing football in empty stadiums is boring – we experienced it during Covid. Cycling is fun if we win a race and cheer with our own team, but it's better if you can celebrate it with the whole fan group that are following you."Back on Ventoux, the race is approaching. There is a cheer running up the mountain, getting louder. When Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney comes into view, solo ahead of Demi Vollering and Marlen Reusser, it erupts into a cacophony: flags waving, cowbells rattling, screaming. It is infectious. The crowd is still cheering when the peloton emerges a few minutes later. Anouska Koster gestures for us to shout louder. Puck Pieterse, wearing her polkadot skinsuit, wheelies through the corner. Alison Jackson takes a hamburger from a fan and holds it triumphantly in the air. With so many people here in the same place, all for the same thing, there is an energy in the air: a crackling connection between fans and athletes that is different from other sports. This bald corner of Mont Ventoux has come alive. And it is certainly more memorable than watching on TV.

item.title: Nicolas Breuillard wins stage 5 of Le Tour de Langkawi as Lennart Jasch keeps firm grip on overall lead in Genting Highlands queen stage
item.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
item.content:encoded: Nicolas Breuillard (TotalEnergies) bounced back from illness earlier in Le Tour de Langkawi to claim the final summit finish of the eight-stage race, winning in the Genting Highlands on stage 5 after dropping his break companion Josh Burnett (Burgos-Burpellet BH) in the final kilometres, and holding off a chase including GC leader Lennart Jasch (Tudor Pro Cycling).On Thursday Jasch, also with the help of the third-place time bonus, extended his lead on Abel Balderstone (Caja Rural-Seguros RGA) to 26 seconds and put Jan Castellon (Caja Rural-Seguros RGA ) 42 seconds behind. It's going to now be hard to budge the first-year professional from that top spot given the flat terrain ahead."The race isn't over yet but we are a big big step closer to the finish line in terms of the GC I would say," said Jasch in a post stage interview.For Breuillard and TotalEnergies, the team of last year's overall winner Joris Delbove, it was a welcome turn of fortunes for the rider and squad. They first had to give their team leader, Jordan Jegat, over as a late replacement for the French team at the Road World Championships, then they lost a retiring Geoffrey Bouchard to a stage 1 crash and then Breuillard had his problems too. "I came here for the GC and I fell sick in the start of the day in Malaysia, after this I wanted to win a stage, and I'm very happy with that," said the French rider, who made his intentions clear on stage 5 when he went out into the break with a teammate Valentin Retailleau alongside, who helped pull out the margin between the peloton and the break to around five minutes at the start of the 22km climb.The 125.7km stage from Tapah to the Genting Highlands started with 111 riders and among those missing was the key GC hope for Picnic PostNL, Mattia Gaffuri, who was caught up in a crash early on stage 4 but rode on and finished with the front group of contenders to retain his seventh spot overall. However, he'd done it with a broken hand."He was really motivated for these two days, but yeah, yesterday, showed a really good spirit to fight to the finish, so he did more than 120k with the hand broken and still held a group of 30 guys," Picnic PostNL sports director Melvin Rulliere told ahead of the stage.That meant there was plenty of incentive for both Picnic PostNL and many other teams that hadn't had the race go their way so far to play an aggressive hand. This was the last chance for the climbers to make a real difference as the road wound its way up through the lush jungle and once again to the top of the climb, which rounded off an otherwise flat stage.The fierce efforts to get in the break even caused a brief split in the peloton at one point, which Jasch was on the wrong side of. Among an early escape there was Matthew Peace (Picnic PostNL), Nicolas Breuillard and Valentin Retailleau of (TotalEnergies) and Mervin Corpuz (7/Eleven Cliqq) but they were pulled back in at 13km to go and then a whole new round of attacking began. Finally a group of six was established up front with Breuillard and Retailleau again part of the group, along with Fernando Gaviria (Caja Rural-Serguros RGA), Josh Burnett and Rodrigo Alvarez (Burgos Burpellet-BH) and Robin Carpenter (Modern Adventure). Edward Cruz (Bardiani CSF 7 Saber) also ultimately made the junction, but not surprisingly sprinter Gaviria fell away as the climbing began. Retailleau, who was working for teammate Breuillard, also fell away after putting in a huge volume of work to set his teammate up with as big a gap as possible, which ended up being five minutes near the bottom of the climb. Others fell away and ultimately it came down to Burnett and Breuillard out the front, with Burnett at times virtually threatening Jasch's lead. However in the final kilometres the Burgos-Burpellet rider from New Zealand fell away from his break companion. Though he didn't let the gap stretch far, holding off the pursuing group behind which Jasch lead over the line. The race leader crossed the line just ahead of Castellon and then a further two seconds back it was José Manuel Díaz (Burgos-Burpellet-BH) and Balderstone.*Cyclingnews attended Le Tour de Langkawi on an invitation/media package from the race that included travel and accommodation. In line with our editorial standards, our coverage is independent and was not subject to review, approval or influence by the organiser or any sponsor; no favourable coverage was promised or given in item.title: Fixer, financier, spymaster: how the UAE’s Sheikh Tahnoon is setting his sights on AI dominance
item.author: Jack Shenker
item.content:encoded: The Emirati royal is increasingly influential on the world stage. Some see him as a visionary. Others compare him to a Bond villain. Who is he?On the night of 12 November 1993, a slim, young Brazilian named Royce Gracie stepped into an octagonal cage in Denver, Colorado, and found himself staring up into the eyes of a giant. Gerard Gordeau, a Dutch kickboxer, stood five inches taller, weighed almost three stone more than him, and had an extra decade of fighting experience under his belt. Now the pair were about to engage in bare-knuckle combat: no judges, no separation of opponents by size, no respite until someone either got knocked out cold or begged for mercy.The fight lasted barely 100 seconds. In that time, Gracie calmly tripped Gordeau up, jumped on his back, and clutched at his throat, forcing the big man to hammer the floor in submission.Continue reading...

item.title: Bahrain Victorious sprinter provisionally suspended by Italian anti-doping authority
item.author: laura.weislo@futurenet.com (Laura Weislo)
item.content:encoded: The Italian Anti-Doping Tribunal (NADT) announced on Wednesday that it has provisionally suspended Alberto Bruttomesso (Bahrain Victorious) for violation of the anti-doping code.The provisions stated in the one-sentence press release list articles 2.1 and 2.2, both related to athlete responsibility for ensuring no prohibited substances enter their bodies.The announcement did not give the date, substance or method involved in the anti-doping rule violation.The 22-year-old has raced with Bahrain Victorious since 2024, and is under contract with the team through 2027.Bahrain Victorious posted a short statement on their website, writing:"Bahrain Victorious is aware of the provisional suspension concerning Alberto Bruttomesso following an anti-doping control conducted by NADO Italia."The team fully supports Alberto throughout the ongoing process and will cooperate fully with the relevant anti-doping authorities as the matter is investigated."While the case remains ongoing, Alberto will be suspended from all team activities pending a clear and definitive outcome from the relevant anti-doping authorities and the completion of the applicable testing and review procedures."Bahrain Victorious remains committed to the highest standards of integrity and to respecting the established anti-doping process. Until that process has concluded, the team will make no further comment."Bruttomesso's case has yet to be registered by the International Testing Agency, the organisation responsible for the majority of testing and results management for professional cycling.Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of both the UCI Road and Gravel World Championships, alongside the final monument of the season, Il Lombardia. item.title: Trump administration diverts human rights funds to push far-right agenda abroad
item.author: Andrew Roth and Joseph Gedeon in Washington
item.content:encoded: Support such as for white Afrikaners and anti-communism reveals how US is redefining what qualifies as human rightsWith hours left before the funding expires, the Trump administration is pushing to direct more than $175m of the state department’s flagship human rights fund to a slate of awards that includes a huge $40m grant for an anti-communism fund, support for a group advancing white Afrikaner rights in South Africa, a campaign against Brazil’s supreme court and programs that would reward ideological allies in Europe who protect “western civilizational norms”.On Wednesday, the state department obligated the funds to the grantees hours before the deadline despite congressional concerns and requests not to do so, according to a source familiar with the negotiations. The state department declined to comment on questions from the Guardian specifically on whether it had obligated the funds and had “blown” holds from Congress due to concerns about the money’s use.Continue reading...

item.title: Knicks enter camp looking to perfect their championship offense
item.author: Russell Richardson
item.content:encoded: You hear versions of the story often. Here’s one that might be apocryphal (forgive me if I get it wrong; I’m bottle-feeding a rescued kitten every two hours and haven’t slept properly since Friday). Rock juggernaut Def Leppard was almost finished recording their follow-up to the multi-platinum , and their track list was locked down when producer Mutt Lange heard singer Joe Elliott strumming something new during a break. Mutt deemed this song a worthy, eleventh-hour addition to the album. That little ditty? “Pour Some Sugar on Me.” Huge hit. Ask your parents.Sometimes a late change, whether accidental or desperate, can alter the fates. In April 2026, the third-seeded New York Knickerbockers found themselves trailing the sixth-seeded Atlanta Hawks two games to one. Our heroes had spent months stress-testing their systems and preparing for a deep playoff run only to get cut up by the honorable, but aging, CJ McCollum.With their backs against the proverbial wall, coach Mike Brown recognized the need for a change. His central adjustment placed Karl-Anthony Towns in a facilitating role farther out from the basket. This reduced the creation load on Jalen Brunson, highlighted Towns’ vision as a passer, drew opposing bigs away from the rim, and created opportunities for the wings to cut and screen effectively.New York’s overall scoring efficiency rose sharply, posting an offensive rating near 124 points per 100 possessions and a record-shattering point differential. Operating in high gear, they went on a 15-1 run that delivered them to the promised land. And there was great rejoicing.Training camp for the 2026-27 season began this week. Now Coach Brown has a chance to refine and expand on his winning formula. Early reports from training camp indicate that Towns’ hub role will remain a priority, as the coaching staff plans to increase elbow involvement for KAT and explore additional ways to involve the wings across the floor. Their options include testing new Knick Andre Drummond as a secondary facilitator and giving OG Anunoby more minutes at center. During the playoffs, OG in particular produced some of his strongest stretches by generating offense off the bounce. Moving him into a small-ball center role with more interior and mid-floor actions could help maximize his impact, especially with limited traditional center depth behind Towns. (Unrelated: OG needs a nickname on his Basketball-Reference page. Help us out.)Coach Brown used the first day of camp to temper expectations that might/can/probably should arise from New York’s legendary postseason finish. He said the regular season will inevitably include adversity and periods when the team does not resemble its postseason peak. Mike has an entire training camp to formalize something that succeeded partly because opponents had little time to prepare for it. Now they know what’s coming. To repeat their championship, the veteran skipper might need a new ace up his sleeve for the next postseason.Maybe that’s why Rajon Rondo appeared at the practice facility this week. Brunson has formed a connection with the two-time champion in recent months and described the former Celtics point guard as a player he watched growing up. As for what he admired, Jalen specifically cited Rondo’s creativity and unusual way of seeing the game.New York may need to explore some fresh ideas if they intend to remain atop the mountain. Sustaining success is difficult in any field, as Def Leppard found out. Almost 40 years later, “Pour Some Sugar on Me” remains their biggest hit. We waited five decades for a championship. We’d rather not wait so long for the next one.

item.title: Knicks sign Tony Bradley and Jaden Akins in training camp roster shakeup
item.author: Michael Zeno
item.content:encoded: The Knicks are not quite done sorting out their training camp roster.On Wednesday morning, as we creep ever closer to next Monday’s preseason opener, the Knicks made a series of roster moves at the back of their training camp roster:Waived John Konchar and N’Faly DanteSigned Tony Bradley to an Exhibit 9 contractSigned Jaden Akins to a two-way contractThere’s a few layers to unpack here, so let’s start with the two new Knicks.You may remember Bradley from his reserve-center minutes for the Indiana Pacers and Atlanta Hawks in the last two postseasons. Picked No. 28 overall by the Lakers in the 2017 draft out of UNC, Bradley will look to make the roster of his seventh team. He started his career as a seldom-used backup big for the Jazz, playing just 12 games total in his first two seasons. He upgraded to being a solid bench player in 2019-20, but then became a complete journeyman.He was traded twice in one week before the 2020-21 season, from Utah to Detroit to Philadelphia, before being shipped out again in March 2021 to the Thunder in a three-team deal that involved the Knicks (the Austin Rivers trade, if you recall). He balled out in 20 games down the stretch, averaging 8.7 points and 6.1 rebounds, the best stretch of his career. After playing 55 games for the Bulls in 2021-22, he hasn’t played more than 41 in a season since. He joined the Pacers in 2024 and was their third center on their run to the NBA Finals, playing 38 minutes total in the Eastern Conference Finals against the Knicks, being a plus-15 in fairly minor action. Bradley found his way to Atlanta midway through the 2025-26 season and played four games in that first-round series too, most notably being minus-17 in the Game 5 blowout.He has a few interesting links to the Knicks aside from the playoffs. He was traded by the Lakers on draft night to Utah for… Josh Hart and Thomas Bryant. When he was sent to Philly in November 2020, it was in a 1-for-1 deal with lottery bust Zhaire Smith, whom the Sixers infamously chose over Mikal Bridges. In that three-team swap in 2021, he was traded with the second-round pick that became Tyler Nickel… to OKC.As for Akins, he’s getting his first NBA opportunity. The former All-Big Ten guard went undrafted out of Michigan State in 2025 and spent the 2025-26 season with the Motor City Cruise, the G League affiliate of the Pistons, where he averaged 14.7 points and 4.4 assists on 41.2% from the field and 35.8% from three.The 23-year-old was with the Knicks in Summer League this year, averaging 11.3 points a night. He was already ticketed for Westchester after signing an Exhibit 10 earlier this month before being subsequently waived, but the Knicks elected to fill their final two-way spot with a guy who’s already in-house.The other two moves could turn out to be just procedural, or could be the sign of the organization going in a different direction.Konchar, the former Grizzlies wing, did not report to training camp with the rest of the roster due to personal reasons. Ian Begley said the motivation for waiving him was to give him more time to deal with his situation, leaving the door open for a potential return down the road. The fact that he said that makes me believe the org thinks highly of him and had him towards the top for consideration for a roster spot.Dante, the former Oregon Duck and brief Hawk and Rocket, was also waived. He is recovering from a torn ACL, and it isn’t surprising if the team deems him more G League fodder, but I found it interesting that he was posted as part of Media Day coverage on Monday. Not sure they’d do that with a guy they had no plans for, so maybe they’ll stash him in Westchester and consider him for a two-way when he’s healthy.Here’s the updated training camp roster:Jalen Brunson, Josh Hart, Mikal Bridges, OG Anunoby, Karl-Anthony Towns, Deuce McBride, Jose Alvarado, Landry Shamet, Andre Drummond, Jordan Clarkson, Tyler Kolek, Pacome Dadiet, Mo DiawaraDrew Eubanks, Bruce Brown, Ochai Agbaji, James Wiseman, Tony BradleyTyler Nickel, Kevin McCullar Jr., Jaden Akins

item.title: Kim Le Court-Pienaar ends season after World Championships crash
item.author: Matilda Price
item.content:encoded: The Mauritian was one of several riders involved in crashes in Montreal over the weekend, but did still manage to finish the race, albeit in 45th place, not the result she may have been hoping for in the climber-friendly race. However, since finishing the race, examinations have revealed a muscular injury that means Le Court-Pienaar will not be able to race the upcoming Italian Classics."Following her crash in the road race at the World Championships in Montréal, further medical examinations confirmed a small tear in her quadriceps," a short statement from her team read. The quadriceps is the muscle at the font of the thigh."After further assessment and in consultation with Kim, the team and the medical staff, it has been decided to bring her 2026 season to an early end and prioritise her recovery. As a result, Kim will not compete in the Italian races as initially planned."She defended her Mauritian road race and TT titles, won a stage of the Tour de France Femmes and finished ninth there, before claiming the overall at the Tour of Britain Women with a win on the Great Orme.She is AG Insurance-Soudal's biggest points-scorer of 2026, consistently landing their biggest wins and she would have been hoping to chase a win in the upcoming Giro dell'Emilia or Tre Valle Varesine. In her absence, and with climbers Urška Žigart and Justine Ghekiere also out of action, AG Insurance will look to riders like Lore De Schepper and the returning Sarah Gigante for their best chances at a result in Italy to round out the season.Le Court-Pienaar will now turn her attention to 2027, where an uninterrupted run at the Ardennes Classics – she was the winner of Liège-Bastogne-Liège two years ago – will likely be a primary goal for the first half of the year. item.title: 'I was just unlucky as hell' - Still no answers as João Almeida hopes to turn around terrible season
item.author: laura.weislo@futurenet.com (Laura Weislo)
item.content:encoded: If there ever was a rider who needed a little good luck, it's João Almeida (UAE Team Emirates-XRG). The 28-year-old's 2026 season has been one misfortune after another.But after coming to a stop in the mixed zone after dropping out of the World Championships road race in Montreal, Almeida had a small red and black polka dot passenger on his left shoulder - a ladybug (or ladybird) - often considered a sign of good luck. Perhaps it means his fortunes will make a turn for the better."I hope you stay here with me," Almeida said to the little beetle after pointed it out.The elite men's road race in Montreal had brought no signs that the Portuguese rider was on the mend. He was dropped on lap 7 of 12 of the hilly 13.3km circuit which normally would be his favoured terrain."I felt really bad, actually, since the start," Almeida said. "I just didn't feel good at all today."It has been a familiar refrain. In March, João Almeida was already searching for answers for why he felt so bad during the Volta a Catalunya. He'd started his season well, with podiums in the Volta Comunitat Valenciana and Volta ao Algarve, but ever since he had to cancel his participation in Paris-Nice due to flu-like symptoms, the whole season has been a struggle.For a rider who has two Grand Tour podiums and has been as high as fourth overall in the Tour de France, the lack of results is baffling."I was just unlucky as hell, to be honest. I crashed in Poland, then I got sick just before Vuelta [a España]. So yeah, my consistency this year in terms of training was basically zero," Almeida said. "I'm always having setbacks, so it's hard to gain some shape like this."His team seemed to catch a little bit of Almeida's curse, with Pogačar crashing out while leading the Vuelta on stage 8, and the team losing three others along the way. "The team supported me a lot, so I'm looking forward to give back some of their efforts and their trust," Almeida said. "It's been tough, but I'll make it."I will do everything I can, like always. I will work hard to be back to normal and hopefully win some races."Almeida is due to represent Portugal at this weekend's European Championships, and maybe he will show that the little spotted passenger has brought him some better fortunes.Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of both the UCI Road and Gravel World Championships, alongside the final monument of the season, Il Lombardia. item.title: 'I do not believe the first is in a mountain stage' – Rare breakaway win for Petr Rikunov in Tour de Langkawi and an 'impossible' return to the KOM jersey
item.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
item.content:encoded: All Petr Rikunov (Wheeltop Rotor Chengdu) had to do was stay out front for the first 9km of the 2026 Tour de Langkawi to sweep up the first and only climbing points available that day and don the Bubbles King of the Mountain jersey on stage 1."It was my easiest job, maybe of all my career," joked Rikunov at the post-stage media conference that day. What he didn't expect to be easy, however, was wearing it again, explaining that with the long finishing climbs starting on the very next stage, "to keep the jersey I think is impossible".And yes, he did lose it on stage 2, but it came right back to him on Wednesday. What's more, to get it back, he took an even bigger prize, the victory on stage 4."It's my first time here, and before it happened my personal goal is to win a stage here, but I do not believe the first is in a mountain stage," said Rikunov, who is not a rider you would categorise as a climber but more a breakaway rider or sprinter.In fact, if Rikunov had more of a reputation on the climbs or had been too close to the top riders on the first climbing stage to Gunung Jerai – rather than 28th and more than five minutes back from the winner – he probably would never have had the opportunity to claim the victory. The team of race leader Lennart Jasch, Tudor Pro Cycling, was only content to give the break such a solid advantage because they weren't an overall threat."Before the last climb, when I saw the gap was two minutes and 30 seconds, for me it was a surprise because the peloton style was just easy and we had a chance for the win in the breakaway," said Rikunov. "The last 5km, I believed it was for the win today."As the three out front – Rikunov, Javier Ibanez (Caja Rural-Seguros RGA) and Alan Jousseaume (TotalEnergies) – were about a kilometre from the line, the Wheeltop Rotor Chengdu rider sensed that there was an earlier opportunity than he'd first anticipated."I wanted to sprint with guys, but in the last kilometres I see the guys' limit, and I think I see a good chance for an attack," said Rikunov.And he certainly made the most of it, surging toward the line and never for a second looking like there was a chance he would be caught. He even had time to sit up and celebrate before Ibanez crossed the line three seconds back and Jousseaume was nine seconds in arrears.It was the first UCI victory for the season for Rikunov, the first time the breakaway prevailed at the race and the first victory for one of the race's Continental squads.That win, and the shift back into the KOM jersey, has left Rikunov with a renewed perspective. While he may not have initially believed there was any chance of taking maximum points for the jersey on the climb, Wednesday proved him wrong."Today again I was in this jersey, and I think it's possible the next day to continue fighting for this jersey, [to] keep it," said Rikunov.*Cyclingnews attended Le Tour de Langkawi on an invitation/media package from the race that included travel and accommodation. item.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘If I get a joint replacement, my career is over’
item.author: Antonio Losada
item.content:encoded: Can you feel it in the air? It’s Knicks basketball scent.New York keeps working through the early days of training camp, gearing up for a preseason matchup with the 76ers on Oct. 5.Meanwhile, here’s the latest we’ve heard about the Knickerbockers inside the Tarrytown facilities and elsewhere.On Andre Drummond being quicker and more explosive than expected:“He’s a little quicker and more explosive.”On Andre Drummond replacing Mitchell Robinson by being himself:“We’re not expecting Andre to come in and be Mitch or impact the game in a lot of different ways that Mitch did. Just be yourself, but everyone else has to step up and box-out a little harder. All those things will make us a top-level team.”On Drummond’s veteran experience, instincts and mobility:“He’s a veteran. He’s been there, done that with a few different teams, and he’s a big body, he’s got great feet. Seems like his instincts are pretty good on both ends of the floor. His feet are quicker than what you could imagine. He’s really light on his feet, which is a good thing.”On the Knicks still discussing a potential White House visit:“No, that’s still something that our guys, the organization, is internally discussing. Whatever we decide to do we’ll all do together.”On his expectations for the Knicksover the 82-game regular season:“We’re not playing at that level for 82 games. You know, we played at a pretty high level, and … that’s not going to happen over 82 games. You know, for me, the 82-game season is about trying to find your way.”On expanding the Knicks’ offense around Karl-Anthony Towns and experimenting with different lineups:“Obviously playing with KAT at the elbow a little bit more than what we did [in the regular season last year]. Being with this group for a year now, you get a better feel of what players can do what. Like I didn’t know if OG could be as effective as he was in the pick-and-roll game. Same with Mikal. So to try to continue to find ways to get those guys involved at the top of the floor is something that we’ll take a look at.“We have great cutters that have tremendous size. We’ll continue to mix that in, and we all know that KAT is a really good facilitator at the elbow. Maybe Andre [Drummond] is too? I don’t know. Maybe we move OG to the five a little bit more than what we did last year. So there are a lot of different ways we can go with the team on both ends of the floor. The biggest thing is knowing that nothing’s set in stone.”On carrying over the Knicks’ playoff offense into the new season while continuing to evolve:“There’s a lot that will carry over for this year. We’ll also experiment with some new things here and there, but the stuff that we had in the playoffs may not work during the regular season. So we have to be ready to evolve or pivot as the year goes along and hopefully come close to playoff time, we’re trending upwards so that we feel we’re in a pretty good spot with the confidence needed to take off from there.”On Andre Drummond’s potential importance to the Knicks:“Can be a big key to this team.”On Drummond replacing Mitchell Robinson by being himself:“Obviously, Mitch was near and dear to all of our hearts. I think the best part of the situation Andre is in, he’s not coming in to be Mitch. He’s coming in to be himself. So we’ve gotta give him the confidence to go out there and be himself.”On getting to know Drummond at his birthday party:“I’ve known him from afar. It’s always been mutual, like hi and bye. Always respect. That was like first time we really got to sit down and have a conversation. It was kind of an icebreaker type of thing.”On his offseason wrist rehabilitation:“I just feel like I didn’t do my normal summer stuff. I feel good, but also I know that it wasn’t just my normal summer.”On how this wrist rehabilitation compared with his previous hand injury:“It was similar, but I was shooting earlier than I was this time. I was in a cast longer than I was before, when I broke my hand. Plus, [surgery] was a little bit earlier — I think I got surgery right after it happened. I didn’t get surgery until like three weeks later [this time] because I didn’t know it was a necessity.”On not viewing his disrupted offseason as catching up:“I don’t want to say I’m catching up. I feel good, but also I know that it wasn’t just my normal summer.”On the praise from LeBron James and Giannis Antetokounmpo:“I really do appreciate it. I respect the hell out of them. It’s honestly really cool … I really do appreciate it, and it shows where I’ve grown, but still got a lot of work to do.”On experiencing the championship summer in New York and finding time to decompress:“It exceeded expectations, honestly. Winning in New York was no joke. It was a really cool experience. … Have I decompressed at all? Not really. I’m gonna be honest with you, not really. But I’ve had times where I had time to relax. I enjoyed that. I spent time getting away from everything. Most times, it was rehabbing. Once I was out of the cast and cleared, I had obligations I had to go through, so I did all of that. But I feel good. And I know where to go to get to my happy place. I know where to go when I need to decompress. I’m good.”On what the Knicks can add to the offense after unlocking something during the playoffs:“I feel like we can do a lot more, do a lot of different things. I think we unlocked something last year in the playoffs at a time of need and it worked. It’s gonna be fun to kind of integrate it from the beginning of the season, too.”On the Knicks learning they need each other to win:“I think as a group, we figured out that we need each other to win, obviously, and we need each other to be on the same page. You never know when things are going to turn for you, when things are gonna click for you. But as long as you keep putting the work in every single day, you keep tapping the rock, tapping the rock, eventually it’s going to break.”On getting to know Rajon Rondo and hosting him at Tarrytown on Tuesday:“I got to talk to him, got to really get to know him this summer. I definitely watched him. He was just so creative and someone who was innovative in the way they play basketball.“Definitely an icon when I was younger. So it was really cool to get to know him and his family.”On Andre Drummond’s rebounding ability:“One of the best rebounders of our generation.”On the freedom he felt after winning the championship:“The ability to celebrate and rejoice and have that joy of a kid without being judged. And also just the freedom of being able to really talk your s— for real, like being able to say you’re the champion and no one being like, well, this or that, whatever.“It was a much more freeing experience now being an adult and being in that situation than I think I would have ever realized when I was young.”On how winning the championship differed from how he imagined it when he was younger:“When you are young, you’re looking at a championship as a sense of accomplishment. I think for me, in that moment winning it, it felt very freeing because a lot of the questions I know people had on me were put to rest.”On refusing to change himself despite outside criticism:“I just was never going to change who I was, even when the world was asking me to change who I was, so I could be the character in their story. I just was going to continue to be me.”On how playing in a smaller market helped his development before arriving in New York:“We talk about (playing in a) small market as a bad thing. It was a great thing for me because it protected me from having to be a perfect form of myself for the big media markets and stuff. I was able to really grow and hone myself as a person and fine-tune the things that I needed to so when I got (to New York), which wasn’t part of my plan, I was truly the best version of myself.”On continuing to work rather than complain about criticism or a lack of immediate success:“I’ve kept my head down and continued to try to be the best human I could be in the world, be the best player I could be even when I needed things to work on. Instead of complaining about why I didn’t get the love or have the immediate success, I just got back in the gym and worked on my game. And this was a year where I finally had enough lessons to really put it together and was given the opportunity to do something special.”On his mother encouraging him to remain himself:“My mom always told me to be who I am and never be ashamed to be who I am. To be unapologetically myself even if the love that I love to show people is not reciprocated.”On mental strength not requiring him to change his personality:“I think mental fortitude and mental strength doesn’t need to come with a frown on it. You can still smile and have an amazing amount of mental strength and have that Mamba Mentality”On preparing for the possibility of being traded to Milwaukee midway through last season:“We were on Zillow looking at Milwaukee. Like, ‘Hey, babe, I went around town, and it’s not that bad. This could be a good spot right here.’”On embracing whatever role the Knicks needed from him during their championship run:“Whatever was needed, I was willing to do at the highest level and be a star in my role. I think, in my career, I’ve always talked about my versatility, and it took that word versatility to get this championship.”On balancing the playoffs with his father’s hospitalization:“That was at the end of the season, too, and I missed every practice; I missed every shootaround. I only showed up to play the games, and I went right back to the hospital. Shoutout to my team.”On finding validation through his own approach:“Is my way the most glamorous way of doing it in the world, especially in the social media world? Absolutely not, because everyone wants instant validation, everyone wants instant gratification. But it is true in the long run, the good guys always win.”On his championship, family and personal life coming together:“My skill, my experience and my personal life all came together at the right moment, at the top, top, top of the game. There’s a lot of euphoria in the Towns family right now.”“A great player. We know he can help us a lot.”On why joining the Knicks made sense for him:“I think it just made the most sense in terms of where I’m at in my career, what this team had just done — they had just won a championship — and with the addition of my veteran leadership and what I bring to the table, it just made sense for me to come here. I had a bunch of different options, but this option was the best one for me. I grew up a Knicks fan from young… So it’s a true honor to put this jersey on.”On taking open 3-pointers without hunting them:“For me, if the shot is there, I’ll take it. It’s not something I’m hunting. Same thing in Philadelphia. It’s not a shot I’m hunting. If it’s a good shot, I will take it.“It’s a shot I’ve worked on. Same thing here. I’ve got the green light to do it. If the shot’s open, take the shot. But my main goal is to help the team the best way I can.”On the skills and durability that have kept him in the NBA:“[I am] a master at what I do. I’m able to rebound the ball at a high clip. Obviously with the addition of the 3-point shot, being able to be a good pick and roll defender, and just being a great locker room guy overall is what keeps me around.“I stay healthy. I take care of my body. I do the necessary things to make sure I’m able to play the game at a high level.”On being the lone newcomer to the Knicks:“This is the first time I’m the only new guy to a team. So it feels kind of weird. Like an outcast trying to fit in but the guys are very welcoming, they made me feel very welcome to be here.“Everybody’s been very nice and showing me the ropes of how to be a New York Knick.”On what he gave Brunson for his birthday:On getting a head start learning the Knicks’ system:“I’ve been here [in Tarrytown], just learning their system and how they flow both on offense and defense. So I’ve got a head start on what’s to come.”On choosing the Knicks in free agency and growing up as a fan:“This was the best option. Being born in Mount Vernon and then moving to Connecticut very young, I’ve always been a Knicks fan — from Amar’e [Stoudemire] to Patrick Ewing, the list of greats in this organization, it’s a true honor to put the jersey on.”On Knicks fans taking over Philadelphia during the playoffs:“It was crazy. It felt like an away game the whole series. They came down and took over the entire arena.“Crazy seeing some of the fans from [Philadelphia] even wearing Knicks jerseys, too, so the Knicks fanbase is just far and wide. It doesn’t matter where you are in the world. It’s the basketball Mecca, so they did what they were supposed to do.”On what he still brings as a veteran center:“I’m able to rebound the ball at a high clip, still. And I’m a very good locker room guy.”On playing with his finger wrapped for the rest of his career:“Just so I don’t got to answer this question anymore. There is no other surgery for me to get besides a joint replacement. If I get a joint replacement, I can’t play with it and my career is over. So it will be wrapped until I retire.”On resolving his past issue with Celtics coach Joe Mazzulla:“At first, we had a little issue because I’m like, ‘You gotta say sorry for fouling me,’ …But he apologized, and now we’re on the same team, so it’s going to be great, just build together and stuff like that, get to know him as the year goes on. I feel like it’s going to be epic.”On refusing to criticize the Knicks this season after their championship:“This year, I will not say a negative word about my New York Knicks. They erased a 53-year drought. They can do no wrong this year to me. They are the reigning, defending NBA champions until further notice, and they will be treated like that on this show by yours truly.”On what he still expects from the Knicks:“You gotta make the playoffs. Can’t stink up the joint, gotta make the playoffs now. Can’t be getting bounced out in the first round.”On not needing LeBron James in New York after the Knicks’ championship:“We don’t need him in New York. But I’m gonna say something on national television that might shock a lot of people. We know that [LeBron] and I don’t mess with each other. We know that story. If the New York Knicks had lost, I would have come on national TV and begged LeBron James to come to the Knicks. I woulda offered to carry LeBron’s bags. I woulda offered to caddy for him, occasionally, while he’s trying to learn golf.“But I am not lying, I am not exaggerating, and I am not engaging in hyperbole. If the New York Knicks had lost in the NBA Finals, I would have begged, and I mean begged, LeBron James to come to New York.”On Karl-Anthony Towns supposedly getting an “unreasonable” offer from the Knicks:“From what I am told — similarly to what Jalen Brunson did — he is also willing to take a pay cut. But the pay cut that the Knicks are asking him to take, he views as unreasonable.”

item.title: The PAS Normal Mechanism Shell Jacket is the 'new sheriff in waterproof cycling jackets' – It's never discounted, so this 15% off reduction is worth grabbing fast
